definition: Connecting a model's output to real, verifiable sources or data instead of letting it answer from memory alone.
details: Grounded systems retrieve documents or query tools, then constrain the answer to what those sources support — which reduces hallucination and makes claims auditable. Retrieval-augmented generation is the most common way to implement it.

explainer.lead: Grounding means making an AI answer from evidence you can inspect, rather than relying only on what the model learned during training. It gives people a way to check claims and reduces the chance of the model inventing information.

tiers.eli5: Imagine answering a quiz with an open textbook instead of guessing from memory. Grounding works the same way: the AI looks up useful information first, then builds its answer from what it finds. You can check the book pages behind the answer instead of simply trusting it.
tiers.practitioner: A typical implementation retrieves relevant documents or calls tools, then passes the results to the generator with instructions to stay within that evidence. Retrieval-augmented generation is the most common approach. The main pitfalls are incomplete or irrelevant retrieval and answers that include claims the supplied evidence does not actually support.
tiers.paperLevel: For a query q, let E be evidence obtained from documents or tools; grounded generation produces an output y = M(q, E) whose claims are constrained to those supported by E. Grounding differs from generation based solely on model parameters, but it cannot guarantee correctness when E is incomplete, irrelevant, or misinterpreted. Its auditable evidence makes unsupported claims easier to inspect.

explainer.example: A user asks, “What does our refund policy say about opened software?” The system retrieves the company’s refund-policy document, finds the section covering opened software, and answers only from that passage while pointing to it as support. If the retrieved policy does not address the case, a grounded answer should acknowledge that rather than invent a rule.

usedIn.name: Document question answering
usedIn.detail: Answers are generated from retrieved passages so readers can check the supporting text.

usedIn.name: Customer support
usedIn.detail: Support answers can be tied to retrieved help documents rather than model memory alone.

usedIn.name: Tool-assisted assistants
usedIn.detail: Assistants can query tools and constrain their responses to the returned information.

explainer.intuition: A model’s memory can fill gaps with plausible-sounding text, so grounding gives it outside evidence to work from. The answer becomes a claim about identifiable sources, not just something the model happens to say.
howItWorks: Take the user’s question or task.
Retrieve relevant documents or query an appropriate tool.
Provide the returned evidence to the model alongside the question.
Generate an answer constrained to claims the evidence supports.
Keep the supporting sources available so claims can be audited.
explainer.whyItMatters: Grounding reduces hallucination by limiting answers to available evidence. It also makes claims auditable, allowing people to inspect the documents or tool results behind an answer.
misconceptions: Grounding does not guarantee truth: retrieved evidence can be incomplete, irrelevant, or wrong.
Adding retrieval is not enough if the generator is still allowed to make unsupported claims.
Grounding is not simply asking a model to sound confident or provide a citation; the source must actually support the answer.
